chunks: Among them is Al-Harith ibn Mudadd al-Juhni, who lived for four hundred years,

and he is the one who said: 'There was no companion on the way from the Hijr to the Safa, nor was there a night-watcher in Mecca. Yes, we were its people, but the passing of nights and the old age (or weariness) of the paths destroyed us.'

key_terms.أَرْبَعَمِائَةِ سَنَةً: Four hundred years, indicating a long lifespan.
key_terms.الْجَدُودُ الْعَوَاثِرُ: The old paths or weariness of the paths, referring to the effects of time and travel.
key_terms.الْحَارِثُ بْنُ مُضَاضٍ: Al-Harith ibn Mudadd, a specific historical figure mentioned in Shia sources.
key_terms.بَيْنَ الْحِجْرِ إِلَى الصَّفَا: Between the Hijr and the Safa, key locations in the Masjid al-Haram in Mecca.
key_terms.صُرُوفُ اللَّيَالِي: The passing/turning of nights, referring to the passage of time.

ai.seo_question: Who is Al-Harith ibn Mudadd al-Juhni and what is his famous poetic verse about Mecca?
ai.summary: In Shaykh al-Tusi’s *Kitab al-Ghayba*, this account of Al-Harith ibn Mudadd al-Juhni serves as evidence for the concept of *Tul al-'Umur* (long lifespans) among pre-Islamic Arabs, linking him to the ancient Jurhum tribe who guarded the Kaaba. His verse poetically laments the transience of worldly power, contrasting the era of his people's dominance with the subsequent solitude of Mecca, a theme resonant with the Quranic narrative of the destruction of past civilizations.
